# Catchment Warning Commons

## Archived Horizon Europe RIA application: abridged Part B

**Submitted: 18 September 2025**  
**Coordinator: Universidad de Valdebruma del Litoral, Spain**  
**Proposed duration: 48 months**  
**Requested EU contribution: EUR 5,100,000**

This archived extract retains the objectives, methodology, implementation structure and resources submitted for evaluation. The anticipated start date in the application was 1 January 2027. The four applicants were Universidad de Valdebruma del Litoral, Institut indépendant d’hydrologie de Rivenne, Instituto Costeiro da Enseada Clara and Associazione dei Comuni delle Acque Civiche.

## 1. Excellence

### Objectives and research questions

Catchment Warning Commons will examine how storm-generated material moves through urban drainage and into estuarine receiving waters, and how forecasts of that movement can inform municipal decisions. Three demonstration catchments, one each in Spain, Portugal and Italy, will connect drainage-outlet forecasts to receiving-water observations. The research question is whether a shared forecasting structure can retain local hydrological detail while supplying information that municipal officers can interpret consistently.

The first objective is to develop a rainfall–runoff forecasting workflow that estimates outlet discharge and suspended-material pulses. The second is to connect those outlet estimates to a receiving-water transport representation. The third is to identify warning formats and administrative arrangements suitable for municipal use. A fourth objective is to compare performance and implementation conditions between the three sites.

The project will retain both the urban source and estuarine receptor. Urban land use affects runoff generation and mobilisation; receiving-water conditions affect the timing and interpretation of contamination signals. Treating either component alone would leave municipal users with an incomplete account of the conditions associated with an alert. The intended outputs are research models, event records, warning demonstrations and administrative guidance.

### Preliminary evidence

The applicants completed Runoff–Reception Ledger with a university award of EUR 420,000. That study recorded 12 storms, four at each catchment. It provided 204 valid suspended-solids samples from 216 scheduled samples and a common structure for relating environmental observations to municipal responsibilities. Mean outlet suspended solids across event means were 86 mg/L, with a 95% bootstrap interval of 61–111 mg/L.

The fitted runoff model produced a discharge root mean squared error of 0.18 m³/s. The application uses this as evidence that the observation and modelling chain can be implemented with available instrumentation. Twenty-four interviews established contacts with technical and administrative officers and documented differences in the organisation of public information. These contacts form the initial user network.

The preceding work did not measure microbial safety or install a public warning service. The new action will investigate the transfer from observation and simulation to a repeatable municipal demonstration. Suspended solids will serve as the first measured transport indicator, with additional contamination indicators considered where local analytical arrangements permit.

### Approach

The environmental work combines rainfall records, drainage representation, level observations, discharge rating information and water sampling. Shared preprocessing will align timestamps, identify event boundaries and attach instrument-quality flags. Site-specific runoff parameters will be estimated before comparison of model structures across catchments. A transport component will receive the predicted outlet hydrographs and material-pulse estimates.

During model development, the existing storm records will be divided into training and evaluation time steps. Selected intervals will be withheld from parameter fitting, while event-level observations will inform choices of lag, runoff representation and preprocessing. Validation will report prediction error on the withheld intervals and agreement between observed and simulated pulse timing. The same event collection will support model selection and demonstrations of warning behaviour.

A new field campaign will seek 36 additional storms, 12 at each site, during the demonstration period. These events will extend the range of rainfall and receiving-water conditions. The proposal does not reserve an untouched event set in advance or distinguish a final external test from continuing parameter adjustment. Performance will be compared periodically as the model is refined.

The social and administrative research will use interviews, workshops and comparative document analysis. Municipal technical officers will review warning displays and discuss which messages are useful. The association will convene exchanges between authorities and prepare guidance. Existing institutional contacts will provide the initial workshop participants. Public-facing communication will use those officers' accounts of residents' information needs.

## 2. Impact

The expected scientific contribution is a common account of the chain from rainfall to outlet response, estuarine transport and public information. The expected administrative contribution is a set of warning demonstrations and procedures that can be adapted locally. The work will compare differences between the three sites rather than impose an identical drainage model.

Municipal uptake will be supported through demonstration meetings, training materials and the association's communications. The application assumes that participating technical departments will identify the relevant operational users as results become available. It does not identify a named official responsible for accepting the system at each site. Warning thresholds will be discussed during the demonstrations; a formal procedure for approving them is not specified.

Equity is treated as a requirement for accessible information. Warning formats will be assessed for clarity and translated for local use. Municipal officers will provide feedback on communication with older residents, residents with limited language proficiency and households in low-lying areas. The work plan contains no separate resident recruitment route, community partnership or compensated co-design activity.

Dissemination will include journal articles, public research summaries and exchanges with water managers. Exploitation will centre on reusable software and administrative guidance. Model code developed by the partners will be released where rights permit. Environmental data will be documented in a data management plan; personal interview material and third-party inputs will remain subject to their respective restrictions. The proposal does not include a commercial service contract or a secured municipal maintenance budget.

## 3. Implementation

The work is organised into five work packages. Coordination and data management run from M1 to M48. Catchment observations and runoff modelling run from M1 to M30. Receiving-water modelling runs from M10 to M36. Municipal demonstrations and warning interpretation run from M25 to M45. Synthesis, training and transfer run from M37 to M48.

Field access and harmonised input data are assumed to be available during the opening phase. The receiving-water component begins before completion of the runoff component, using provisional outputs. Municipal demonstrations begin while both components remain under refinement. The risk register recognises delays in obtaining observations, but the submitted schedule does not assign a specific duration or funded owner to every interface check, installation permission or software handover.

Valdebruma coordinates the action and leads planning analysis. Rivenne leads hydrological modelling and shared computational processing. Enseada Clara leads receiving-water work and laboratory coordination. Acque Civiche leads municipal exchanges, training and administrative comparison. The partners will meet regularly to resolve interface requirements. The budget provides technical effort within partner totals without a separate estimate of each deployment dependency.

### Submitted resources

The requested contribution is allocated as follows: Valdebruma EUR 2,040,000; Rivenne EUR 1,275,000; Enseada Clara EUR 1,020,000; Acque Civiche EUR 765,000. The total is EUR 5,100,000. The application requests reimbursement at 100% of eligible costs for the four nonprofit applicants.

The aggregate cost estimate comprises EUR 3,060,000 personnel, EUR 1,020,000 other direct costs and EUR 1,020,000 indirect costs. The indirect estimate is 25% of EUR 4,080,000 eligible direct costs. No subcontracting is included. Other direct costs cover field equipment, consumables, laboratory access, travel and demonstration activities; they are not accompanied by a dependency-level procurement schedule.

Work-package allocations are EUR 510,000 for coordination and data management, EUR 1,530,000 for catchment observations and modelling, EUR 1,275,000 for receiving-water modelling, EUR 1,020,000 for municipal demonstrations, and EUR 765,000 for synthesis and transfer. These allocations sum to the same requested contribution. The final transfer activities extend through M48.

# European Commission — Evaluation Summary Report

**Proposal title:** Catchment Warning Commons  
**Type of action:** Horizon Europe Research and Innovation Action  
**Coordinator:** Universidad de Valdebruma del Litoral  
**Submission date:** 18 September 2025  
**Report date:** 12 February 2026

## Evaluation result

| Criterion | Score | Threshold |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Excellence | 3.0 / 5 | 3 |
| Impact | 3.0 / 5 | 3 |
| Quality and efficiency of the implementation | 2.5 / 5 | 3 |
| Total | 8.5 / 15 | 10 |

The proposal does not reach all evaluation thresholds and is not recommended for funding. Scores are awarded to each criterion as a whole. The comments below form the consensus assessment.

## Criterion 1 — Excellence

The objectives are relevant and generally clear. The proposal addresses the connection between urban runoff and estuarine receiving waters and recognises that environmental information must be interpreted within municipal procedures. The combination of field measurements, modelling and administrative research is appropriate to this problem. The previous observations demonstrate that the partners can collect and organise comparable event records.

However, the validation methodology does not adequately separate model development from evaluation. Time steps described as withheld belong to storms that have already informed parameter choices, preprocessing and model selection. Consequently, the reported fit and the proposed interval-based tests do not establish independent forecasting skill. The new event campaign is not accompanied by a locked held-out-event allocation, an explicit rule preventing subsequent tuning on test events, or criteria for deciding whether performance supports demonstration. This is a significant shortcoming because credible warnings depend on performance outside the calibration collection.

The proposed link to receiving-water transport is scientifically relevant. Its assessment will depend on a clearer account of how uncertainty propagates through the coupled components, within the validation approach described above.

## Criterion 2 — Impact

The proposed outputs could be useful to municipal water managers and the association provides a credible route for professional exchange. The dissemination activities and comparison across administrative settings are appropriate. Open release of permitted software and documentation is positively assessed.

Nevertheless, municipal adoption is insufficiently substantiated. No responsible operational owner is identified for accepting or maintaining the demonstrations, and no decision threshold is linked to an authorised municipal action. Workshops and training alone do not establish an adoption route. The proposal leaves unclear who would accept a false-alarm burden, approve escalation or decide that a forecast is unsuitable for use.

In addition, underserved and vulnerable residents are absent from the co-design arrangements. Their needs are represented through municipal officers rather than through direct participation or a justified alternative. There is no recruitment pathway or provision addressing barriers to participation. The stated equity objective is therefore not supported by the activities and resources described.

## Criterion 3 — Quality and efficiency of the implementation

The consortium brings complementary competence in planning, hydrology, coastal processes and municipal administration. The distribution of broad scientific responsibilities is reasonable. The principal cost categories and partner totals are internally consistent.

However, the modelling and deployment dependencies are not adequately timed or costed. Receiving-water modelling and demonstrations depend on drainage inputs, permissions, interface checks and stable upstream outputs whose availability is assumed. Several handovers have no responsible delivery role, duration or identifiable resource provision. The schedule overlaps modelling and deployment without adequate gates or contingency, making the feasibility of the demonstrations and final transfer uncertain. This shortcoming is not resolved by the general coordination arrangements.

## Additional assessment

The proposal does not request an exception to the applicable funding conditions. No additional funding recommendation is made. The scientific evaluation does not constitute approval of ethics arrangements, data permissions or municipal operating authority.

# Method and dependency review record

**Technical board meeting: 22 July 2026**  
**Amendment approved: 23 September 2026**

Participants were the four institutional leads and the partner staff responsible for instruments, data stewardship and training. The board reviewed the February evaluation, the archived scripts and work completed under existing institutional duties. No external award financed this review. The decisions concern method documentation and the status of the collaboration's working records.

## Event-validation protocol

Rivenne deposited protocol version 1.0 on 19 June 2026. The university data steward recorded its version identifier and read-only copy on the same date. The protocol was written after all 12 historical storms had been examined. It therefore classifies those storms as development evidence and prohibits relabelling any of them as unseen validation events.

The protocol defines an event as the complete rainfall–runoff episode, including its recession and associated receiving-water observations. All observations from an event remain together. Where one weather system affects more than one study catchment, the associated records are grouped for partitioning. This prevents an apparently independent test from containing another part of the same storm system.

For a prospective collection of 18 eligible storms, the protocol specifies six per site, with three development and three held-out events at each site. Allocation follows a pre-recorded sequence before laboratory results or model errors are inspected. Eligibility concerns instrument coverage and event completeness, not favourable model performance. Exclusions require a reason recorded before outcome inspection. The nine held-out events remain unavailable to model developers until preprocessing, parameters and analysis code are locked.

The evaluation specification includes error in peak discharge, pulse-arrival timing, interval coverage and event-level warning outcomes. Comparisons use a simple persistence or rainfall-threshold baseline fixed before release of held-out data. Forecast intervals must propagate observation and parameter uncertainty. Event-level uncertainty and site-level results are retained even where pooling would produce a more precise-looking estimate.

An internal research gate requires an improvement over the baseline whose event-bootstrap uncertainty interval excludes no improvement. Failure leads to classification as an unsuccessful research demonstration, not post hoc adjustment of the same test set. A test invalidated by data leakage requires a fresh independent collection. The protocol also requires reporting the width and coverage of predictive intervals; a narrow interval alone is not evidence of utility.

This statistical gate is not a municipal operating threshold. Acceptance of missed-event and false-alarm consequences belongs to an authorised decision process, which has not been completed. Transfer between sites is specified as a separate leave-one-site-out analysis with destination-site outcomes excluded from fitting. With only three sites, its conclusions remain exploratory.

No prospective storms have been enrolled, no held-out set exists and no protocol execution has occurred. The written protocol addresses the design of an independent test; it supplies no evidence that the coupled system passes that test.

## Completed dependency analysis

The board examined a reduced configuration using 18 prospective storms instead of the archived application's 36, a single transport indicator, research demonstrations and existing partner institutions. It removed the continuous operational-service demonstration and the extended post-demonstration transfer phase. These are boundaries of a completed feasibility analysis, not approved purchases or funded field commitments.

The resulting map has a 36-month envelope. Input permissions, installation access and measurement specifications occupy M1–M6. Event acquisition occupies M7–M24. Model development and interface work occupy M7–M21, with code and preprocessing locked at M21. Held-out evaluation occupies M25–M30; administrative interpretation, bounded demonstrations and synthesis conclude during M31–M36. No funded-work assumption in this map extends beyond M36.

The map explicitly places permissions before installation, quality control before event allocation, outlet-interface acceptance before receiving-water testing, and evaluation before demonstrations presented as evidence of skill. Records collected for the held-out set before M21 remain sequestered. Insufficient eligible storms by M24 trigger a reduced evidential claim, rather than an automatic extension or reuse of development storms.

The analysis assigned institutional owners to these handovers and identified technician time, laboratory processing, translation, accessibility support, data stewardship and software maintenance as resource requirements. Their amounts have not been priced. Procurement lead times and maintenance cover remain unconfirmed. The shorter dependency map cannot be treated as a proportionate reduction of the earlier budget.

## Status at closure

The board accepted the protocol and dependency map as current internal records. The liaison assignment and signed organisational agreements are documented in the consortium record. There are still no independent validation results, approved municipal operating thresholds, completed resident sessions or replacement financial schedule. The record distinguishes completed preparatory work from the empirical and administrative decisions that remain outstanding.

**Project period: 1 January 2022–31 December 2024**  
**Final report accepted: 28 February 2025**  
**Evidence-status update: 16 September 2026**

Principal investigator: Elena Sorlí Valderra, Universidad de Valdebruma del Litoral. Collaborating institutions: Institut indépendant d’hydrologie de Rivenne, Instituto Costeiro da Enseada Clara and Associazione dei Comuni delle Acque Civiche.

The university's Territorial Systems Research Fund awarded EUR 420,000 under reference UVL-TS-2021-17. Recorded expenditure was EUR 250,000 for personnel, EUR 60,000 for instruments and consumables, EUR 45,000 for laboratory analysis, EUR 30,000 for travel and transcription, and EUR 35,000 for institutional support. These amounts total EUR 420,000. European Union contribution: EUR 0. Closing balance: EUR 0.

The project examined whether a common event record could connect urban runoff measurements, receiving-water observations and the responsibilities described by municipal staff. Its deliverables were an observational collection, analysis scripts and a comparative administrative study.

## Sites and measurement design

Three study catchments were coded A, B and C in the shared research files. They lie respectively on the eastern Spanish coast, the Portuguese Atlantic coast and the northern Italian Adriatic coast. Each includes an urban drainage outlet connected to an estuarine receiving reach. Detailed access coordinates are withheld in the public documentation because some observations were made from restricted maintenance sites.

The measured drainage areas were 2.1, 3.4 and 2.8 square kilometres. Their differing outlet geometry, tidal influence and drainage maintenance histories prevent interpreting them as replicate experimental units. The project obtained observations during 12 storms, four per catchment, between October 2022 and November 2024. Collection used manual timed sampling and depended on safe staff access. The collection excludes the most severe locally reported flooding.

Each storm contributed six timed sampling rounds at three stations: an upstream drain, the outlet and an estuarine receiving station. This produced 216 scheduled water samples. Twelve samples were excluded because of bottle damage or inadequate sample volume, leaving 204 valid suspended-solids measurements. All storms retained at least one valid measurement at each station. Fifteen-minute level records and discharge rating observations were associated with the sampling rounds. The event, rather than an individual time step or bottle, was the unit used for uncertainty estimation.

## Numerical findings

The mean outlet suspended-solids concentration across the 12 event means was 86 mg/L, with a 95% event-bootstrap interval of 61–111 mg/L. Each event mean was calculated first, so events with more surviving bottles did not receive greater weight. The estimate describes the sampled events rather than annual average conditions.

For the fitted rainfall–runoff model, discharge root mean squared error was 0.18 m³/s, with a 95% event-bootstrap interval of 0.12–0.25 m³/s. The calculation pooled residuals within events and resampled whole events for the interval. These are in-sample fit statistics: parameters and processing choices had been informed by every one of the 12 storms.

Turbidity observations supported the timing of suspended-material pulses, but the relationship with laboratory suspended solids differed between sites. The receiving-water work compared the order and approximate timing of observed pulses at outlets and estuarine stations. Sparse sampling and tidal reversals prevented reliable attribution of a concentration peak to an individual urban source. A transferable estuarine transport model remains unestablished.

The measured transport endpoint was suspended solids. Microbial, nutrient and chemical-toxicity endpoints were outside the analytical programme. Suspended-solids concentrations therefore provide no direct measure of recreational-water microbiological safety.

## Administrative study

The qualitative component comprised 24 semi-structured interviews with municipal technical or administrative employees, eight in each study country. The analysis used a shared coding guide and a second-reader review of passages concerning responsibility for action. Eighteen interviewees could identify an office that distributed environmental information; six could identify a documented route from a model output to an authorised operational decision. These are interview findings rather than an audit of legal competence.

Recruitment used institutional contacts and included municipal employees only. Interview consent covered research analysis and anonymised quotation. The resulting material describes staff perceptions and administrative arrangements; it does not provide residents' accounts of warning comprehension or household response capacity.

The Runoff–Reception Event Ledger release package contains event summaries, an instrument dictionary and analysis scripts. Public summaries exclude restricted source layers and personal data. Input permissions and transcript access are recorded in the separate resources register.

### Objectives and research questions

Catchment Warning Commons will examine how storm-generated material moves through urban drainage and into estuarine receiving waters, and how forecasts of that movement can inform municipal decisions. Three demonstration catchments, one each in Spain, Portugal and Italy, will connect drainage-outlet forecasts to receiving-water observations. Our research question is whether a shared forecasting structure can retain local hydrological detail while supplying information that municipal officers can interpret consistently.

The first objective is to develop a rainfall–runoff forecasting workflow that estimates outlet discharge and suspended-material pulses. The second is to connect those outlet estimates to a receiving-water transport representation. The third is to identify warning formats and administrative arrangements suitable for municipal use. A fourth objective is to compare performance and implementation conditions between the three sites.

The project will retain both the urban source and estuarine receptor. Urban land use affects runoff generation and mobilisation; receiving-water conditions affect the timing and interpretation of contamination signals. The intended outputs are research models, event records, warning demonstrations and administrative guidance. Their common event structure will allow partners to trace an observation from rainfall and drainage conditions through to the information presented to a municipal user.

### Preliminary evidence

The applicants completed Runoff–Reception Ledger with a university award of EUR 420,000. That study recorded 12 storms, four at each catchment. It provided 204 valid suspended-solids samples from 216 scheduled samples and a common structure for relating environmental observations to municipal responsibilities. Mean outlet suspended solids across event means were 86 mg/L, with a 95% bootstrap interval of 61–111 mg/L.

The fitted runoff model produced a discharge root mean squared error of 0.18 m³/s. The observation and modelling chain was implemented using the partners' field instruments and computational facilities. Twenty-four interviews established contacts with technical and administrative officers and documented differences in the organisation of public information. These contacts form the initial user network.

The action will extend this work from observation and simulation to a repeatable municipal demonstration. Suspended solids will serve as the first measured transport indicator, with additional contamination indicators considered where local analytical arrangements permit. Comparing the timing of outlet and receiving-water pulses will help identify where local tidal and drainage conditions require separate parameterisations.

### Approach

The environmental work combines rainfall records, drainage representation, level observations, discharge rating information and water sampling. Shared preprocessing will align timestamps, identify event boundaries and attach instrument-quality flags. Site-specific runoff parameters will be estimated before comparison of model structures across catchments. A transport component will receive predicted outlet hydrographs and material-pulse estimates.

During model development, the existing storm records will be divided into training and evaluation time steps. Selected intervals will be withheld from parameter fitting, while event-level observations will inform choices of lag, runoff representation and preprocessing. Validation will report prediction error on the withheld intervals and agreement between observed and simulated pulse timing. Performance on the withheld intervals will be re-assessed after each model refinement.

A new field campaign will seek 36 additional storms, 12 at each site, during the demonstration period. These events will extend the range of rainfall and receiving-water conditions. Successive event records will be incorporated into model comparison as laboratory results become available. The expanding collection will support adjustments to the model and examples of warning behaviour under contrasting conditions.

The social and administrative research will use interviews, workshops and comparative document analysis. Municipal technical officers will review warning displays and discuss which messages are useful. The association will convene exchanges between authorities and prepare guidance. Existing institutional contacts will provide the initial workshop participants. Municipal officers will relay the needs of older residents and households in low-lying areas, drawing on their experience of local communications and service delivery.

# Elena Sorlí Valderra

**Curriculum vitae updated 25 September 2026**

Professor of Urban Water Planning, Department of Architecture and Territorial Systems, Universidad de Valdebruma del Litoral, Spain. Institutional base: Valencia. Research interests: drainage infrastructure, spatial planning and water management, and the administrative conditions under which environmental forecasts become public decisions.

## Education and employment

Elena Sorlí Valderra completed her architecture degree at Universidad de Valdebruma del Litoral in 2001 and her doctorate in territorial planning at the same institution in 2007. Her doctoral research examined how drainage maintenance responsibilities were represented in municipal land-use documents. It combined analysis of planning instruments with interviews and field inspection.

She held a postdoctoral research appointment at the university from 2007 to 2010, was lecturer from 2010 to 2015, associate professor from 2015 to 2022, and has held her present permanent professorship since September 2022. Her appointment includes research, teaching and departmental administration. Her teaching covers planning evidence, infrastructure governance and research ethics in public-space studies.

## Research leadership

Sorlí Valderra was principal investigator of Runoff–Reception Ledger, a university-funded research project running from 1 January 2022 to 31 December 2024. Its EUR 420,000 award supported field measurements, laboratory work and interviews in three coastal urban catchments. The financial and scientific reports were accepted by the university research committee on 28 February 2025.

She coordinated Catchment Warning Commons, submitted as a Horizon Europe Research and Innovation Action on 18 September 2025. The application was unsuccessful following evaluation in February 2026. Her European collaboration experience comprises joint research agreements and proposal coordination.

Within Runoff–Reception Ledger she supervised the integration of drainage observations with documentary evidence about municipal responsibilities. Hydrological parameter estimation was led by Bastien Delvaux Orsanne, and receiving-water analysis by Madalena Seabra Valmouro. Sorlí Valderra managed the shared reporting process and chaired meetings at which the partners reconciled environmental and administrative records.

## Supervision and professional contribution

She has supervised four completed doctorates, awarded in 2015, 2018, 2021 and 2025, and currently supervises two doctoral candidates. Their topics concern drainage maintenance in planning documents and the accessibility of environmental information.

She chaired the consortium's technical review on 22 July 2026 and approved its amended dependency record on 23 September 2026. # Runoff–Reception Ledger: final scientific report

**Project period: 1 January 2022–31 December 2024**  
**Final report accepted: 28 February 2025**

Principal investigator: Elena Sorlí Valderra, Universidad de Valdebruma del Litoral. Collaborating institutions: Institut indépendant d’hydrologie de Rivenne, Instituto Costeiro da Enseada Clara and Associazione dei Comuni delle Acque Civiche.

## Award and objectives

The university's Territorial Systems Research Fund awarded EUR 420,000 under reference UVL-TS-2021-17. Recorded expenditure was EUR 250,000 for personnel, EUR 60,000 for instruments and consumables, EUR 45,000 for laboratory analysis, EUR 30,000 for travel and transcription, and EUR 35,000 for institutional support. These amounts total EUR 420,000. European Union contribution: EUR 0. Closing balance: EUR 0.

The project examined whether a common event record could connect urban runoff measurements, receiving-water observations and the responsibilities described by municipal staff. Its deliverables were an observational collection, analysis scripts and a comparative administrative study.

## Sites and measurement design

Three study catchments were coded A, B and C in the shared research files. They lie respectively on the eastern Spanish coast, the Portuguese Atlantic coast and the northern Italian Adriatic coast. Each includes an urban drainage outlet connected to an estuarine receiving reach. Detailed access coordinates are withheld in the public documentation because some observations were made from restricted maintenance sites.

The measured drainage areas were 2.1, 3.4 and 2.8 square kilometres. Their differing outlet geometry, tidal influence and drainage maintenance histories prevent interpreting them as replicate experimental units. The project obtained observations during 12 storms, four per catchment, between October 2022 and November 2024. Collection used manual timed sampling and depended on safe staff access. The collection excludes the most severe locally reported flooding.

Each storm contributed six timed sampling rounds at three stations: an upstream drain, the outlet and an estuarine receiving station. This produced 216 scheduled water samples. Twelve samples were excluded because of bottle damage or inadequate sample volume, leaving 204 valid suspended-solids measurements. All storms retained at least one valid measurement at each station. Fifteen-minute level records and discharge rating observations were associated with the sampling rounds. The event, rather than an individual time step or bottle, was the unit used for uncertainty estimation.

## Numerical findings

The mean outlet suspended-solids concentration across the 12 event means was 86 mg/L, with a 95% event-bootstrap interval of 61–111 mg/L. Each event mean was calculated first, so events with more surviving bottles did not receive greater weight. The estimate describes the sampled events rather than annual average conditions.

For the fitted rainfall–runoff model, discharge root mean squared error was 0.18 m³/s, with a 95% event-bootstrap interval of 0.12–0.25 m³/s. The calculation pooled residuals within events and resampled whole events for the interval. These are in-sample fit statistics: parameters and processing choices had been informed by every one of the 12 storms.

Turbidity observations supported the timing of suspended-material pulses, but the relationship with laboratory suspended solids differed between sites. The receiving-water work compared the order and approximate timing of observed pulses at outlets and estuarine stations. Sparse sampling and tidal reversals prevented reliable attribution of a concentration peak to an individual urban source. A transferable estuarine transport model remains unestablished.

The measured transport endpoint was suspended solids. Microbial, nutrient and chemical-toxicity endpoints were outside the analytical programme.

## Administrative study

The qualitative component comprised 24 semi-structured interviews with municipal technical or administrative employees, eight in each study country. The analysis used a shared coding guide and a second-reader review of passages concerning responsibility for action. Eighteen interviewees could identify an office that distributed environmental information; six could identify a documented route from a model output to an authorised operational decision. These are interview findings rather than an audit of legal competence.

Recruitment used institutional contacts and included municipal employees only. Interview consent covered research analysis and anonymised quotation. The resulting material describes staff perceptions and administrative arrangements.

## Research record

The Runoff–Reception Event Ledger release package contains event summaries, an instrument dictionary and analysis scripts. Public summaries exclude restricted source layers and personal data. Input permissions and transcript access are recorded in the separate resources register.

## 1. Excellence

### Objectives and research questions

Catchment Warning Commons will examine how storm-generated material moves through urban drainage and into estuarine receiving waters, and how forecasts of that movement can inform municipal decisions. Three demonstration catchments, one each in Spain, Portugal and Italy, will connect drainage-outlet forecasts to receiving-water observations. Our research question is whether a shared forecasting structure can retain local hydrological detail while supplying information that municipal officers can interpret consistently.

The first objective is to develop a rainfall–runoff forecasting workflow that estimates outlet discharge and suspended-material pulses. The second is to connect those outlet estimates to a receiving-water transport representation. The third is to identify warning formats and administrative arrangements suitable for municipal use. A fourth objective is to compare performance and implementation conditions between the three sites.

The project will retain both the urban source and estuarine receptor. Urban land use affects runoff generation and mobilisation; receiving-water conditions affect the timing and interpretation of contamination signals. The intended outputs are research models, event records, warning demonstrations and administrative guidance. Their common event structure will allow partners to trace an observation from rainfall and drainage conditions through to the information presented to a municipal user.

### Preliminary evidence

The applicants completed Runoff–Reception Ledger with a university award of EUR 420,000. That study recorded 12 storms, four at each catchment. It provided 204 valid suspended-solids samples from 216 scheduled samples and a common structure for relating environmental observations to municipal responsibilities. Mean outlet suspended solids across event means were 86 mg/L, with a 95% bootstrap interval of 61–111 mg/L.

The fitted runoff model produced a discharge root mean squared error of 0.18 m³/s. The observation and modelling chain was implemented using the partners' field instruments and computational facilities. Twenty-four interviews established contacts with technical and administrative officers and documented differences in the organisation of public information. These contacts form the initial user network.

The action will extend this work from observation and simulation to a repeatable municipal demonstration. Suspended solids will serve as the first measured transport indicator, with additional contamination indicators considered where local analytical arrangements permit. Comparing the timing of outlet and receiving-water pulses will help identify where local tidal and drainage conditions require separate parameterisations.

### Approach

The environmental work combines rainfall records, drainage representation, level observations, discharge rating information and water sampling. Shared preprocessing will align timestamps, identify event boundaries and attach instrument-quality flags. Site-specific runoff parameters will be estimated before comparison of model structures across catchments. A transport component will receive predicted outlet hydrographs and material-pulse estimates.

During model development, the existing storm records will be divided into training and evaluation time steps. Selected intervals will be withheld from parameter fitting, while event-level observations will inform choices of lag, runoff representation and preprocessing. Validation will report prediction error on the withheld intervals and agreement between observed and simulated pulse timing. Performance on the withheld intervals will be re-assessed after each model refinement.

A new field campaign will seek 36 additional storms, 12 at each site, during the demonstration period. These events will extend the range of rainfall and receiving-water conditions. Successive event records will be incorporated into model comparison as laboratory results become available. The expanding collection will support adjustments to the model and examples of warning behaviour under contrasting conditions.

The social and administrative research will use interviews, workshops and comparative document analysis. Municipal technical officers will review warning displays and discuss which messages are useful. The association will convene exchanges between authorities and prepare guidance. Existing institutional contacts will provide the initial workshop participants. Municipal officers will relay the needs of older residents and households in low-lying areas, drawing on their experience of local communications and service delivery.

## 2. Impact

The expected scientific contribution is a common account of the chain from rainfall to outlet response, estuarine transport and public information. The expected administrative contribution is a set of warning demonstrations and procedures that can be adapted locally. The comparison will retain differences between sites in drainage geometry, tidal conditions and administrative practice.

Municipal uptake will be supported through demonstration meetings, training materials and the association's communications. Participating technical departments will identify operational users as results become available. Thresholds will be agreed with participating technical departments during the demonstrations. Workshop discussions will consider how officers interpret uncertainty and what information they require before escalating a warning.

Equity is treated as a requirement for accessible information. Warning formats will be assessed for clarity and translated for local use. Municipal officers will provide feedback on communication with older residents, residents with limited language proficiency and households in low-lying areas. Their comments will inform the wording and presentation of demonstration messages.

Dissemination will include journal articles, public research summaries and exchanges with water managers. Exploitation will centre on reusable software and administrative guidance. Model code developed by the partners will be released where rights permit. A data management plan will describe environmental data, documentation and access conditions. Interview material and third-party inputs will be managed under their respective consent and licensing arrangements. Training materials will include worked examples that can be discussed within municipal departments.

## 3. Implementation

The work is organised into five work packages. Coordination and data management run from M1 to M48. Catchment observations and runoff modelling run from M1 to M30. Receiving-water modelling runs from M10 to M36. Municipal demonstrations and warning interpretation run from M25 to M45. Synthesis, training and transfer run from M37 to M48.

Opening activities will assemble field-access documentation and harmonise input data. The receiving-water component will begin with provisional runoff outputs, allowing development to proceed alongside the catchment work. Municipal demonstrations will use successive versions of the coupled workflow. Regular partner meetings will review model changes, field progress and requirements emerging from user discussions. Delayed observations will be managed through adjustments to field scheduling and the sequence of demonstration examples.

Valdebruma coordinates the action and leads planning analysis. Rivenne leads hydrological modelling and shared computational processing. Enseada Clara leads receiving-water work and laboratory coordination. Acque Civiche leads municipal exchanges, training and administrative comparison. Each lead will report progress and resource use to the coordinator at the project meetings.

### Submitted resources

The requested contribution is allocated as follows: Valdebruma EUR 2,040,000; Rivenne EUR 1,275,000; Enseada Clara EUR 1,020,000; Acque Civiche EUR 765,000. The total is EUR 5,100,000. Reimbursement is requested at 100% of eligible costs for the four nonprofit applicants.

The aggregate cost estimate comprises EUR 3,060,000 personnel, EUR 1,020,000 other direct costs and EUR 1,020,000 indirect costs. The indirect estimate is 25% of EUR 4,080,000 eligible direct costs. No subcontracting is included. Other direct costs cover field equipment, consumables, laboratory access, travel and demonstration activities. Partner administrators will monitor expenditure against these categories throughout implementation.

Work-package allocations are EUR 510,000 for coordination and data management, EUR 1,530,000 for catchment observations and modelling, EUR 1,275,000 for receiving-water modelling, EUR 1,020,000 for municipal demonstrations, and EUR 765,000 for synthesis and transfer. Final training and transfer activities will consolidate the demonstration experience into documented research workflows and municipal guidance.

## Criterion 1 — Excellence

**Score: 3.00 (Threshold: 3/5.00, Weight: -)**

The objectives are relevant and generally clear. The proposal addresses the connection between urban runoff and estuarine receiving waters and recognises that environmental information must be interpreted within municipal procedures. The combination of field measurements, modelling and administrative research is appropriate to this problem. The previous observations demonstrate that the partners can collect and organise comparable event records.

However, the validation methodology does not adequately separate model development from evaluation. Time steps described as withheld belong to storms that have already informed parameter choices, preprocessing and model selection. Consequently, the reported fit and the proposed interval-based tests do not establish independent forecasting skill. The new event campaign is not accompanied by a locked held-out-event allocation, an explicit rule preventing subsequent tuning on test events, or criteria for deciding whether performance supports demonstration. This is a shortcoming because credible warnings depend on performance outside the calibration collection.

The proposed link to receiving-water transport is scientifically relevant. Its assessment will depend on a clearer account of how uncertainty propagates through the coupled components, within the validation approach described above.

## Criterion 2 — Impact

**Score: 3.00 (Threshold: 3/5.00, Weight: -)**

The proposed outputs could be useful to municipal water managers and the association provides a credible route for professional exchange. The dissemination activities and comparison across administrative settings are appropriate. Open release of permitted software and documentation is positively assessed.

Nevertheless, municipal adoption is insufficiently substantiated. No responsible operational owner is identified for accepting or maintaining the demonstrations, and no decision threshold is linked to an authorised municipal action. Workshops and training alone do not establish an adoption route. The proposal leaves unclear who would accept a false-alarm burden, approve escalation or decide that a forecast is unsuitable for use.

In addition, underserved and vulnerable residents are absent from the co-design arrangements. Their needs are represented through municipal officers rather than through direct participation or a justified alternative. There is no recruitment pathway or provision addressing barriers to participation. The stated equity objective is therefore not supported by the activities and resources described.

## Criterion 3 — Quality and efficiency of the implementation

**Score: 2.50 (Threshold: 3/5.00, Weight: -)**

The consortium brings complementary competence in planning, hydrology, coastal processes and municipal administration. The distribution of broad scientific responsibilities is reasonable. The principal cost categories and partner totals are internally consistent.

However, the modelling and deployment dependencies are not adequately timed or costed. Receiving-water modelling and demonstrations depend on drainage inputs, permissions, interface checks and stable upstream outputs whose availability is assumed. Several handovers have no responsible delivery role, duration or identifiable resource provision. The schedule overlaps modelling and deployment without adequate gates or contingency, making the feasibility of the demonstrations and final transfer uncertain. This shortcoming is not resolved by the general coordination arrangements.

## Event-validation protocol

Rivenne deposited protocol version 1.0 on 19 June 2026. The university data steward recorded its version identifier and read-only copy on the same date. The protocol classifies all 12 historical storms as development evidence.

An event is the complete rainfall–runoff episode, including its recession and associated receiving-water observations. All observations from an event remain together. Where one weather system affects more than one catchment, its records are grouped for partitioning. The allocation register records both the site-event identifier and the weather-system identifier.

The prospective target is 18 eligible storms: six per site, comprising three development and three held-out events at each site. Allocation follows a pre-recorded sequence before laboratory results or model errors are inspected. Weather-system grouping takes precedence over site quotas. Eligibility concerns instrument coverage and event completeness. Exclusions require a reason recorded before outcome inspection. The target is nine held-out events, sequestered by the data steward until preprocessing, parameters and analysis code are locked.

The evaluation specification covers peak-discharge error, pulse-arrival timing, predictive-interval coverage and event-level warning outcomes. Observation and parameter uncertainty pass through both runoff and receiving-water components. The forecast experiments specify 15-minute and 30-minute horizons, conditional on timestamped rainfall inputs passing the latency and coverage checks. Each forecast must use only information available at its issue time. Experiments driven by subsequently observed rainfall are recorded separately as hydrological hindcasts.

The baseline is fixed before release of held-out data. A primary loss measure is selected in the analysis specification, with secondary measures reported alongside it. The internal research gate requires an improvement over the baseline whose event-bootstrap uncertainty interval excludes no improvement. Failure is recorded as an unsuccessful research demonstration. Leakage invalidates the affected test and requires fresh independent evidence. Predictive-interval width and coverage are reported together.

Transfer is examined separately through leave-one-site-out analysis, excluding destination-site outcomes from fitting. With three sites, this analysis is exploratory. The research gate and the administrative acceptance threshold occupy separate fields in the evaluation record.

At the September amendment, the protocol had not been executed: prospective collection had not begun and the data steward had received no held-out events. External review of the protocol was still pending.

## Sampling-feasibility amendment

The field team reviewed permitted gauge summaries for the 12 complete calendar years 2012–2023. Applying the rainfall criterion used in the earlier campaign identified 96 candidate episodes at A, 108 at B and 84 at C: annual rates of 8.0, 9.0 and 7.0 respectively. Approximate 95% Poisson intervals were 6.5–9.8, 7.4–10.9 and 5.6–8.7 episodes per year. These intervals exclude interannual clustering and uncertainty in the rainfall criterion.

The earlier manual campaign secured four complete sampled storms per site over approximately 26 months. The board therefore treated staff access and capture completeness as constraints separate from rainfall occurrence. For an 18-month acquisition window, the historical rates imply 12.0, 13.5 and 10.5 candidate episodes. A provisional 65% usable-capture assumption gives expected usable counts of 7.8, 8.8 and 6.8, rounded to one decimal place. This assumption has not been measured locally.

The equipment requirement supporting that assumption is three automatic water samplers, one at each outlet, with event triggering, secure power, sample preservation and timely laboratory collection. Upstream and receiving-water rounds still require safe access. The samplers are identified requirements, with quotations and procurement lead times outstanding. The expectation of six eligible events per site remains conditional on installation and capture performance; the board did not assign a probability of completing all site quotas.

Unpriced requirements comprise automatic sampling equipment, installation and servicing, technician time, laboratory processing, rainfall-input acquisition, translation, accessibility support, data stewardship and software maintenance.
